title: Hot Cocoa Mix

drivers.name: Memorial Day (holiday)
drivers.evidence: Noise-adjusted effect from 2 past occurrences: x0.85 vs baseline; 2024 was an outlier (x0.49), 2025 was x0.9.

drivers.name: 20% off promotion
drivers.evidence: No prior 20% off event; 25% off in Apr lifted x1.22, 30% off in Jan lifted x1.18; lift likely capped at x1.20 due to diminishing returns and noise.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 19.6. Memorial Day historically lowers sales (noise-adjusted x0.85), but the 2024 data point (x0.49) is an outlier. The promotion is 20% off—deeper than past 10–25% discounts, but no past 20% off event exists. The noise-adjusted lift from past promotions is x1.08, but the 30% off in Jan 2026 lifted sales only 18% (x1.18), and the 25% off in Apr lifted 22% (x1.22). The deeper discount this week may not yield more than 1.2x. However, the classical model underestimates due to overlapping effects and lack of context. The post-promo dip (x0.75) is irrelevant here as this is the promotion week. Combine holiday (x0.85) and promotion (x1.20), but shrink toward 1.0 due to limited evidence on this discount depth. Final median adjusted for both drivers.

  shelf price: 4.02 (-20.1% vs regular price 5.03)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 19.6 | 5%-95%: 1.3 - 33.4 | 10%-90%: 9.3 - 32.4

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-37% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
